title: Should I develop art for my game first, or complete the game and swap in my art at the very end.

posts.author: Thornyan64
posts.body:
I want to create an RPG but was averse to using RPGMaker in order for the game not to look so "RPGMaker-ey". I eventually settled on RPGMaker as I'm used to creating scripts, variables, common events, etc. now. I am a complete noob when it comes to pixel art, yet I want to try to create some instead of using the RTP in order for my game to stand out (I am aware that this could take a long time). I've received advice from others that when it comes to making games, you should make small games and prototypes before working on the super long dream game, but I wonder: if I were to finish a prototype game completely using the RTP, how easy would it be to at the end swap my own art into the RTP? This would mean the map sprites and overworld character sprites. Would it be possible for me to just edit the existing files at the end, or do you foresee something going wrong?
Long story short: I want to follow the advice of others and start off small, but if I finish a small game and find that I want to publish it, would I have to recreate the entire thing with the new art or would I be able to just swap in my art? If the latter is true, what would be the easiest way to do this/pitfalls I should watch out for?
(Also, I plan on using GIMP to create my art, but if you have any other suggestions then please let me know!)

posts.author: alice_gristle
posts.body:
Swapping in new art is no big trouble, so I wud do it that way!
Just make sure you keep the old filenames when you doin' swappin'

posts.author: alice_gristle
posts.body: Also, I'm a GIMP user, but I don't think it's super good for pixel art. People have been sayin' good things about Aseprite, so check that out maybe?

posts.author: RCXGaming
posts.body: Always complete your game first. It complicates the process in a few nasty ways if you try to make art when you don't even have a finalized draft of what the game is going to be like. (eg. having to make new art when you realize you can't use this current art anymore, etc.)

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
I would usually suggest making your actual game using RTP assets as placeholders first for a multitude of reasons.
One very cynical reason is that many, many RPG Maker users never actually finish a game. And if you can't finish your game, then time spent making assets is sort of wasted if they will never be used.
The exception to that cynical reason is if you are having fun and enjoying what you are doing. For instance, I love learning how to make things in RPG Maker. So, if I never actually finish a game, that is ok because I enjoyed the experience.
The same is true with art. If you enjoy the process and enjoy learning how to do it, then it isn't wasted time. Even if your art never gets put into a game.
So what I would say is to balance your time to stay interested in things. Maybe focus on making the mechanics/functionality/story etc. of the game, but also take some time to practice and improve on your art skills.
I have seen a number of users on this forum who have started learning pixel art while they are making their games and that is a good process.
After all, becoming good at something usually requires practice. So if you wait to delve into the new skill of pixel art until your game is mostly done, then you still have that long road of learning and practice ahead of you.
But if you start practicing a little at a time and continue to steadily improve, by the time you get to a point where you are ready to replace assets, you will either be ready to jump in with both feet or you will already have some assets that you like and want to use.
Regardless, good luck on your projects and remember to enjoy what you do!

posts.author: Ms Littlefish
posts.body: Yeah, broken record. Change it out later. I definitely doodle and sketch a lot, but…too much can change. The amount of times I’ve tweaked a character outfit or scrapped an entire location idea is insane.

posts.author: bgillisp
posts.body:
I make the game first and swap it out later. Until the game is done just find something that doesn't make your eyes bleed.
Just prepare for people to miss the note that it is placeholders if you release a demo. I used the maid character for a placeholder in a demo and got a few comments of "Why is Sarah in a maid outfit?". To which I had to refer them to the above post about placeholders.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Mirroring everyone else:
Swap it out later.
Several reasons for this (even a few I didn't see mentioned):
1.  Your project will change over the course of its lifecycle.  The story will change.  The characters will change.  The locations will change.  Etcetera.  Creating new art every time something changes is a good way to spend too much money on your project or waste too much time on it to the point you never finish it.
2.  Keeping a list of what you need as you create a game is far more efficient than adding the artwork "as you need it".  Need some sprites that kiss?  Put a note down.  Need sprites that kiss here.  Need a different kind of forest here, because it's Silverwood trees, where the leaves are blue and the wood is actual silver?  Make a note you need that and swap it later.  A list is easier and faster to change than actual artwork.  This will actually teach you how to organize your project, too.
3.  If you swap correctly, you won't really need to "redesign" anything.  You'll just need to change the pathway for what you're referencing.  This isn't really a lot of time in comparison to the rest of your game.  Especially if you just go down the list of each map.
4.  Most people never complete their RPG Maker games.  There are, in fact, several hundred I've seen over the years on this website who get locked in the loop of "just keep making new artwork", rather than completing the game.  I used to call these people "not devs", because they weren't.  The only part of game design they wanted to do was "make the artwork", so they'd scrap projects frequently to make new art, new characters, etcetera.  Their time would've been better spent creating assets and selling them to people who ACTUALLY WANTED to make a game, rather than pretending they wanted to make one, and spending all their time on artwork instead.  There are "writers", "plugin creators", and "system creators" who are the same on this website.  They make the thing they want to make, then scrap their project to do it all again.  These people would better serve the community through being assets to it, rather than pretending they actually want to make a game... because they don't.  They just like the small niche thing they do in relation to game design.  Swapping out artwork once the game is done, is a good way to figure out if you're a "not dev" or a dev.
Please note, there is nothing wrong with being a "not dev".  A lot of great "not dev" users contribute here in very amazing ways.  We couldn't operate without many of them.  But, it's good to know whether you care about actually making a game, or just a small section of a game.
5.  If you save and budget money every week during game development, you can then have money for art assets later.  I personally sock away $5 per week for future art assets (over the course of 10 years, you can imagine how much money I've got sitting in an account for a game I will very likely never finish).  This budget can be used to directly purchase assets or to pay for classes or... whatever.  This gives you some breathing room for "polishing" your project.  Then you won't be posting, "Hey, I need a character sheet for free", and can instead come in with "I can afford a character sheet for up to $15, but no more" and you can shop around a lot better.
6.  If you save the artwork for the end, then the entire game will have the aesthetic.  Or, a similar aesthetic.  You won't have low quality assets in one area and then high quality ones in another.  Aesthetics are very important.  More important thatn "sprite looks good" is "all sprites look like they go together".  If you want the defintion of "bad aesthetics", then go look at Final Fantasy 7.  Polygonal sprites on matte paintings looks awful.  Polygonal sprites with photorealistic spells looks awful.  On and on.  You will avoid "clashing aesthetics" if all your artwork is created at the same time or all bought from the same person.
